description: We'e a pre-formed team of friends driven by our shared fascination with space missions, orbital mechanics, and video game design/development. Our strengths lie in collaborative problem-solving, creative ideation, and great team communication. We’re  really excited to tackle challenges inspired by the cosmos! Note: Our roster is currently full and we are not looking for new team members at this time, but we’re excited to connect with other space and gaming enthusiasts during the event!
summary:
Space missions are balancing acts: a better instrument adds science, but also mass, power, data and cost. Students rarely experience a whole mission, so these trade-offs stay abstract. Shackleton Prospector is a game where you design and operate a robotic mission to Shackleton crater on south pole of the Moon, collect samples to search for evidence of water, and return them to Earth.
It can be played solo, guided by four animal mentors, or cooperatively with up to four players, each with a private panel and a voice channel to negotiate. The animals embody the real roles: the Andean Condor, who surveys the horizon, directs the mission; the Ovenbird, which builds its nest piece by piece, manages mass and power; the Southern Right Whale, whose songs cross oceans, handles communications; the Jaguar, a patient tracker of clues, leads science.
It turns abstract systems engineering into a tangible, end-to-end experience: every component choice creates operational consequences and recovery options, and random incidents inspired by real missions test each design.
It matters because it bridges theoretical STEM education and real mission operations, teaching students how interdisciplinary teams manage uncertainty, balance competing priorities and diagnose root causes when spaceflight doesn't go to plan.
details:
What it does and how it works

The game can be played solo or cooperatively with up to four players, and unfolds in seven phases: concept and scenario, design and review, integration and testing, launch and cruise, landing, surface operation, and ascent and return. Before each flight, the team (or the solo player) learns the landing site and expected conditions, then chooses equipment from a catalog where every part declares its cost, mass, volume and power use. Shared budgets update live, so each choice visibly takes margin from another area of the mission. In team mode, each player takes the role of one animal and sees only their own panel, so teammates use a built-in voice channel to share information, negotiate competing priorities and agree on decisions. In solo mode, the player makes every decision while the four animals act as advisors, each offering guidance from their own specialty and pointing out the trade-offs the others would raise. Before launch, every subsystem must be confirmed, and safety conditions are mandatory: they cannot be waived.

During the mission, each game draws a random but physically coherent scenario (lighting, terrain, launch weather) and schedules one incident for each of the four specialties. Players (or the solo player, guided by the advisors) solve them in 60 to 120-second mini-games following four steps: detect, diagnose, act and verify. The equipment chosen earlier changes the options available in these challenges.

The game is played as a single complete mission, from concept to recovery, so every early decision carries through to the end. The mission ends with the capsule, samples and data recovered on Earth, or with an autopsy that explains the root cause of any failure and what would have helped.

Benefits

Shackleton Prospector makes the logic of real mission design tangible. Players discover that every decision has a consequence: an extra battery helps survive the lunar night but adds mass and cost and may force a bigger launcher, while a backup antenna rescues communications at a lower data rate. Because no single design is perfect, players compare options, accept risks and justify their choices to teammates. Failure is treated as part of the process: a post-mission autopsy connects scenario, equipment, agreements and incidents to explain what went wrong and what would have helped. The game is also accessible, with a friendly tone for beginners and young players. Solo or team play, with a built-in voice channel for teams, lets it work in a classroom, at home or remotely.

Intended impact

We want to narrow the gap between theoretical STEM education and real mission operations. Students rarely see a mission from concept to recovery; here they experience systems engineering as a whole and learn that no subsystem can be optimized in isolation. In team mode, by giving each player a private view and a voice channel, the game also trains communication, negotiation and shared responsibility, the skills interdisciplinary teams rely on to manage uncertainty and diagnose root causes. By using Argentine animals as characters, we also hope to make space engineering feel closer and more welcoming to young people in our region, and to spark curiosity about careers in science, engineering and mission operations.

Tools and technologies

The game runs in the browser, built with HTML and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D visuals. The backend is written in Python and hosted on Microsoft Azure, and Supabase provides the database. We used ChatGPT to generate images and code, and Claude to support design, writing, code and also to generate some of the sounds used. The physics models (rocket equation, energy, thermal, communications link and navigation) are simplified but based on real principles, with references from NASA, JPL and JAXA.

Creativity

Each discipline of mission design becomes a character: the Condor, Ovenbird, Whale and Jaguar mirror real roles instead of appearing as menu options. In team mode, collaboration is a core mechanic, not an add-on: information is truly distributed across private panels, so teams must talk, as real teams do. In solo mode, the animals become advisors with their own personality. Incidents adapted from real missions (Mars Climate Orbiter, SLIM, Voyager 2, Galileo, LCROSS, OSIRIS-REx) turn historical lessons into mini-games built around detect, diagnose, act and verify. Random scenarios are physically coherent, so no two missions are alike and nothing happens by magic.

Factors considered

Scientific rigor (no resource disappears by chance; difficulty changes demand, not rules), reproducibility (saved seeds to compare designs) and accessibility (a friendly tone for beginners and young players).
